svg.data-vd-steps: [[0, "Lead(II) bromide is heated until it melts, so its ions are free to move. Solid ionic compounds do not conduct."], [2, "When the current is switched on, electrons flow through the wires from the anode to the cathode."], [3.5, "Positive lead ions move to the negative cathode; negative bromide ions move to the positive anode."], [6.5, "At the cathode: Pb\u00b2\u207a + 2e\u207b \u2192 Pb. Lead ions gain electrons (reduction); molten lead forms."], [9, "At the anode: 2Br\u207b \u2192 Br\u2082 + 2e\u207b. Bromide ions lose electrons (oxidation); brown bromine gas forms."], [11.5, "Remember OIL RIG: oxidation is loss of electrons (anode), reduction is gain (cathode)."]]
svg.title: Electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide
svg.desc: A d.c. supply connected to two inert electrodes in molten lead(II) bromide. Lead ions move to the cathode and form lead; bromide ions move to the anode and form bromine.
svg.text: Inert (graphite) electrodes. Ions and electrons drawn much larger than real.

g.data-info: Pushes electrons from the anode, round the circuit, to the cathode.
An ionic compound must be molten or dissolved so its ions are free to move and carry the charge.
Positive electrode. Negative ions (anions) are attracted; they lose electrons: oxidation.
Negative electrode. Positive ions (cations) are attracted; they gain electrons: reduction.
Lead(II) bromide is heated until it melts (about 373 °C).
Move to the cathode: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb. Molten lead collects at the bottom.
Move to the anode: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻. Brown bromine gas is given off.
Electrons flow through the wires only; in the electrolyte, the charge is carried by moving ions.
